Design notes

Source: vignettes/articles/design.Rmd
design.Rmd

xrdbi is small, and most of what it does follows from a few decisions. This article records them and the reasons for them.

A connection is a handle to a live object

The “database” is an xarray Dataset in a Python session that R reaches through reticulate, and the connection is a handle to that object. DBI gives the vocabulary:

  • tables are variables, data variables and coordinates alike
  • fields are a variable’s dimensions, then its other coordinates, then the variable itself: the columns of its rows
  • a statement is a Python expression over ds and xr

The dplyr layer adds grids: the variables on one set of dimensions, read as one table with a column each, as tidync reads them. DBI’s tables stay variables; xr_grids() lists the grids and tbl() takes their names. Grid tables are where the byterefs plan vocabulary meets xrdbi: members of a grid share its selection, and xr_chunks() maps that selection to chunk rows keyed dim_0 .., as byterefs tables are.

Nothing of xarray is ported or wrapped: xarray opens the data, selects it, and computes on it, with every engine and index it has. xrdbi adds the mapping to rows, and the guards.

Python is the query language

A statement is Python, not SQL, because xarray’s selection language already says what array queries need: labels, positions, slices, nearest-neighbour lookups, pointwise selection, and any computation after. A SQL dialect would be a smaller language that compiles to the same thing.

xr_query() and the dplyr verbs are compilers to that language, and their output is a plain string that show_query() prints and dbGetQuery() runs like any other. The compiled expression is the contract: it can be read, logged, kept with a result, and run by hand. Where a compiler cannot express something, the statement can, and params passes R values into it by name instead of pasting them into source.

The long form is xarray’s

A result renders as to_dataframe().reset_index() would give it: one row per cell, every coordinate a column. That is xarray’s own long form, with its column order and broadcasting, so a result means the same in R as in Python, and nothing about it is xrdbi’s invention.

The rows are built in R. Only the values cross from Python, column by column, and the coordinate columns are repeated with rep() for the rows asked for. That is faster than converting a pandas frame (in our measurements, ten million rows in about half a second, where reticulate’s conversion of one pandas datetime column took about two seconds per million rows) and more faithful: each column keeps its type, and NaT becomes NA.

The data frame is one rendering of a result, not the result. xr_raster() renders the same statement as pixels with a georeferencing attribute, and xr_chunks() renders the storage under it. The array, the rows, the raster and the chunk map are views of one selection.

Lazy where xarray is lazy

dbSendQuery() evaluates the statement, and a selection reads nothing there, because xarray’s arrays are lazy until their values are needed. The first fetch reads. A statement that computes runs when it is sent, because that is when Python evaluates it; xrdbi does not pretend otherwise. The documentation says so rather than trying to guard it, and the advice is to select first, then compute.

Guards, not surprises

The stores xarray opens can be enormous: a whole variable of the ERA5 reanalysis is over a trillion cells. Every read that materializes cells is sized first and refused above a limit, ten million cells by default, with the size in the message. The limit is an option and an argument, and force = TRUE reads anyway. xr_chunks() has its own limit on rows, since a store can have a million chunks.

A veneer, not a jail

xr_dataset() returns the Dataset and xr_module() the xarray module, unconverted, so anything the DBI methods cannot express is one step away. A connection can also adopt any Dataset built in Python. xrdbi never needs to be the only way in.

Pixels here, chunks elsewhere

xrdbi gives pixel-level rows on demand from anything xarray can open. The chunk-level view of an array store, as a relation of chunk keys, byte ranges and encoded blobs with grid math done client-side, is deliberately a different project, sketched in the design note DBI for xarray. xr_chunks() is the bridge: it maps the storage chunks under a selection from metadata alone, without reading data. storecard works on the metadata side of the same question: a small description of an array store’s grid, chunking and byte locations, built without reading a data chunk.

Not yet

  • summarise() compiled to xarray reductions in the dplyr layer
  • streaming fetch aligned to chunks: dbFetch(n = ) builds only the rows asked for, but the first fetch reads the values of the whole selection
  • DataTree groups as schemas: open = "open_datatree" connects, but the table listing assumes a flat Dataset
  • writing: dbWriteTable() as to_zarr(), or an icechunk commit
  • transactions: dbBegin(), dbCommit() and dbRollback() error for now. The intended mapping is icechunk sessions and commits, where a readonly session at a snapshot is an AS OF query
  • a switch for coordinates in renderings: 2-D coordinates are broadcast into every row of a variable, which is faithful but can be heavy
  • registry integration: dbConnect(xarray(), sds::dsn("oisst")), where a registry entry carries the open function and its arguments
